“I have been in this mountain longer than your current kingdom has had a name.”

“You really know how to make a person feel urgent.”

“You are urgent.”

That caught me.

“The Line?”

“No.”

I stared.

Ithar's eye stayed on me.

“You are sixty soon.”

“Thank you.”

“Your species measures a life in decades and then behaves surprised when there are not enough of them.”

“I am not surprised.”

“No?”

“No.”

The answer came too quickly.

His eye sharpened.

I regretted it immediately.

I regretted it immediately.

“Interesting,” he said.

“Don't.”

“You have been searching for me for years.”

“We covered that.”

“You are not surprised by the scarcity of a human lifetime.”

“That is called being fifty-nine.”

“You have already lived two.”

“I told you not to do that.”

“And you arrived with enough food to reach me, not enough to return.”

“I can hunt.”

“With your leg.”

“Yes.”

He waited.

“Poorly.”

“Your planning prioritizes arrival over departure.”

“I came here to save the Line.”

“Perhaps.”

“Your planning prioritizes arrival over departure.”

“I came here to save the Line.”

“Perhaps.”

The word sat badly between us.

I looked at the passage again.

The exit did not help.

“What if I say no?”

“You leave.”

“That's it?”

“Yes.”

“No fire.”

“Not for refusing conversation.”

“Again, excellent qualifier.”

“You may die on the mountain.”

“I know.”

“You may live.”

“I know.”

“The Line may fail.”

My jaw tightened.

“I know.”

Ithar watched that one land.

Then, for once, he did not press.

“There is water behind the second stone shelf.”

“I hear it.”

“There are animals below the eastern face.”

“The cliff?”

“The other eastern face.”

“Helpful.”

“I can show you.”

I blinked.

That might have been the first practical offer he had made me.

Not save the kingdom.

Not repair the Line.

Food directions.

It was a start.

“You'd let me stay here?”

“Yes.”

“For months.”

“If months are required.”

“You understand I have to sleep.”

“Yes.”

“Eat.”

“Yes.”

“Shit.”

“Yes.”

“Yes.”

“Eat.”

“Yes.”

“Shit.”

“Yes.”

“Good. Just establishing the hospitality package.”

“You are welcome to shit outside.”

I laughed.

Ithar did not.

Maybe that was a joke.

I was beginning to think the problem was not that dragons lacked humor.

The problem was that this one did not care whether I noticed.

I finally unbuckled my pack.

My shoulder loosened the moment the weight came off.

I set the pack beside the stone and sat properly.

The leg thanked me.

I finally unbuckled my pack.

My shoulder loosened the moment the weight came off.

I set the pack beside the stone and sat properly.

The leg thanked me.

The rest of me felt like I had just signed something without reading the last page.

Ithar settled too.

The cave changed around his weight.

For a while neither of us spoke.

I thought about the Line.

I thought about the road down.

I thought about Nhal beneath the salt flats.

I thought about a kitchen that had not existed for thirty years and then had.

A woman's hand.

A child's laugh.

A wooden leg leaning against a bed because the socket had rubbed the skin raw that day.

I stopped there.

Not yet.

Ithar's nostril moved.

He had heard the silence change again.

“Where does the discrepancy begin?” he asked.

I looked at him.

“Nineteen.”

“Then begin there.”

I rested my hands on my knees.

Both of them felt old.

Only one had been old the first time.

“Fine.”

The word came out smaller than I expected.

I took a breath.

And remembered waking up.
